common_name: Blue Barlow Columbine (Double Spurless Violet-Blue Granny's Bonnet)

planting.note: Sow outdoors in fall for natural cold stratification, or chill seed several weeks before spring sowing; blooms the second year.

directions: A member of the Barlow series bred alongside Nora Barlow and Black Barlow, this selection carries the same fully double, spurless pompom flowers but in rich violet-blue rather than pink or near-black. Grow it in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in dappled woodland shade or morning sun, where its blue-green divided foliage and nodding flower heads pair well with ferns and hostas. Like other Barlow types it comes substantially true from seed in isolation, but open pollination near single-flowered columbines will gradually dilute the double form in self-sown offspring. Deadhead spent stems to tidy the plant, leaving a few seed heads if you want it to naturalize.

common_name: White Barlow Columbine (Double Spurless Ivory Granny's Bonnet)

planting.note: Sow outdoors in fall for natural cold stratification, or chill seed several weeks before spring sowing; blooms the second year.

directions: This is the pale counterpart to Black Barlow and Blue Barlow, producing dense, spurless double flowers in soft ivory-white above the same ferny, blue-green foliage typical of European columbine. Site it in light shade or morning sun in moist, well-drained soil amended with leaf mold or compost, and mulch to keep roots cool through summer. Plants are short-lived but readily self-sow; because columbines cross freely, isolate from other colors if you want seedlings to hold the double white form. Watch for leaf miners and powdery mildew in humid climates and thin crowded clumps every few years to maintain airflow.

planting.note: Sow in early spring after chilling seed, or start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; also suited to fall sowing for cold stratification.

directions: A very dwarf strain of the Japanese fan columbine, Cameo forms tight mounds only a few inches tall topped with upward-facing, short-spurred flowers in blue-and-white or rose-and-white bicolors, making it one of the smallest columbines widely offered from seed. Its compact habit suits rock gardens, trough plantings, and container culture where taller columbines would overwhelm the design. Grow in gritty, well-drained but moisture-retentive soil in morning sun with afternoon shade, since both waterlogging and prolonged heat stress this smaller-rooted selection. It flowers the first year from an early sowing and is generally shorter-lived than species columbines, so collect and resow seed or treat plantings as needing periodic refreshing.

common_name: Clementine Dark Purple Columbine (Double Spurless Clematis-Flowered Columbine)

planting.note: Sow outdoors in fall for natural cold stratification, or chill seed several weeks before spring sowing; blooms the second year.

directions: Part of the Clementine series bred for spurless, fully double flowers that resemble small clematis blossoms rather than a typical nodding columbine, this selection opens in deep violet-purple above lacy, blue-green foliage. Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in partial shade, where the flat-faced double blooms show especially well in a woodland edge or cottage border. It is somewhat shorter and more compact than old-fashioned single columbines, making it useful toward the front of a shaded bed. As with other double columbine strains, isolate from single-flowered types to keep self-sown seedlings true, and divide or replace clumps every few years as plants naturally decline.
